📢 Our new Deloitte Thought Leadership paper on financing the energy transition is now available online. In this paper, we study the reason why the investments in the green technologies are below what is needed to stay in line with climate goals and we identify the key policy and financial tools to boost these investments, especially in developing economies. 

💡 The analysis in this paper goes beyond finance to help provide a holistic overview, employing quantitative modelling and qualitative assessment of the technology landscape, policy environment, and financing challenges, without missing the geographical dimension.

📰 My key takeaways:
▶Governments, investors, and financial institutions must work together to  reduce risks and unlock private capital at attractive costs, especially in developing economies, where about 75% of the investments should take place.
▶While significant upfront investments are needed (4.3% to 5.7% of global GDP in the short run), the cost of inaction is even higher (8% of global GDP).
▶Improved financing structures could reduce the cost of the transition by 25% (US$50 trillion) over the period to 2050. 

🔗 Click on the following link to find out more about the study: https://lnkd.in/gtqkud_A 🤘 Bravi to my co-authors: Bernhard Lorentz Johannes Trüby Pradeep Philip Clément Cartry Clémence Lévêque Vincent Jacamon Will Symons Brice Chasles Dr. Gildas de Muizon Freedom-Kai Phillips

Reflecting on #COP28 in Dubai, it's evident that the conference signifies a crucial starting point, but substantial efforts are still imperative to avert a 1.5°C temperature rise. The urgency transcends mere negotiations; it underscores the need to secure financing promptly for a swift transition to a decarbonized world.

At the core of achieving decarbonization objectives lies the imperative to minimize risks and their associated costs, emphasizing the pressing nature of the situation. The clarion call is unequivocal—intensify endeavors in renewables, triple efficiency, and substantially augment climate finance.

Acknowledging the magnitude of the challenge, reliance on public finance alone proves inadequate. This is an all-encompassing moment that requires collaboration with both multilateral and national development banks to strengthen their role in channeling and delivering climate finance along with domestic and international public and private finance. Equally pivotal is the active engagement of the private sector in steering this transformative journey. 

On the COP sidelines, discussions with officials from Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Maldives, Nepal, Ethiopia, Vietnam, Zimbabwe, Senegal, Azerbaijan and Togo, along with UNDP representation at key events, underscored a shared vision for change. From elevating ambitions in NBSAPs to championing nature-based solutions and just energy transformation, the common thread is clear—change is possible and already underway.

In essence, post-COP28, we stand at the threshold of transformative action, and the next steps demand collective commitment and collaborative action from all stakeholders to turn the tide towards a sustainable and decarbonized future.

With a robust $5 billion portfolio, UNDP actively collaborates with 140 countries on nature, climate, and energy initiatives. Our work with civil society organizations and Indigenous Peoples will be crucial for these efforts. 

Let’s work together to expedite progress, success hinges on the urgency of our responses.

As the year comes to a close, I would love to reflect on a period marked by remarkable achievements and meaningful progress with the Arab Youth For COP . This year has been a testament to the dedication, resilience, and impact of our initiative as we achieved a significant milestone. Our delegation, comprising ten fellows from various Arab countries, effectively implemented our programs, a testament to our commitment to climate action and sustainable development. The journey to COP28 UAE  was enriched by our pre-conference efforts, notably our participation in the #menaclimateweek held in Riyadh. The successful implementation of our programs and the meaningful engagement of our 10 fellows at COP28 underscore our commitment to representing diverse voices, especially those from regions facing conflict, occupation, or marginalization.

Central to our preparatory phase were comprehensive capacity-building sessions. These sessions, led by experts like Mr. Kamal Djemouai  on negotiation principles and Riad Meddeb  alongside his team at the UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub, focused on just transitions and green jobs. But also some sessions on leadership skills sessions by other partners. This groundwork was crucial in equipping our fellows with the necessary skills and knowledge to navigate the complexities of climate negotiations and advocacy.

At COP28, our primary focus was on fostering meaningful engagement for our current fellows as well as alumnus. We created platforms enabling them to voice the concerns and aspirations of their communities.This approach ensured that diverse perspectives were represented and heard, an essential aspect of inclusive and effective climate action.

As we conclude this year’s mission, our eyes are set on the future. We are already laying the groundwork for next year’s initiatives. We are deeply committed to sustaining and expanding our programs, and in this spirit, we are open to exploring partnerships and collaborations. 

We believe that through collective effort and shared knowledge, we can create a more sustainable and equitable future. Therefore, we warmly invite you to join us in this endeavor. Your support, be it through expertise, resources, fund, capacity building, or advocacy, would be invaluable in our journey towards a just greener, more resilient world. 

Absolutely, a heartfelt thank you is due to everyone who played a part in this year’s success. Our partners’ invaluable contributions and our fellows who deserve immense appreciation for their dedication and enthusiasm. And of course, a special acknowledgment to our own team Neeshad Shafi  Amal Ridene  and Omnia El Omrani, MD  Small in size but monumental in impact, each member’s dedication, creativity, and perseverance have been the cornerstone of our achievements.

This year of success is not just an end but a beacon for future endeavors, inspiring us to continue our journey with more vigor and determination.

As part of the 12th Forum of Small States (FOSS) Fellowship Programme, we had the pleasure of hosting the Permanent Representatives to the UN from Botswana, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Fiji, Grenada, Kyrgyzstan, Lesotho, Micronesia, Nauru, Senegal, Suriname and Tuvalu, in our office yesterday.

We also connected with Yemesrach Workie from the UNDP Pacific Office in Fiji, framing the path forward for continued collaboration on digital transformation and strategic innovation. We look forward to strengthening cooperation and supporting the developmental aspirations of small states.

repost-6efc216751db0e19268b.sharedText:
#AI for #ClimateAction- A balancing act between opportunities & perils of artificial intelligence in #climatechange. 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBvAjRsn
 
I am excited to share my new podcast on “AI solutions for Cimate Actions & Insights from #COP28 with @Carina Schuster 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBvAjRsn  
@Sci-Tech Suisse Podcast
 
AI can do great things to fight climate change:
 
✅ The use of data-driven AI solutions can produce starting results in the fight against climate change
 
✅ Data and AI platforms can be powerful instruments to predict weather, track #GHG emission or develop targeted strategies against #airpollution or support the protection of #biodiversity and endangered #species

✅ AI tolls can accurately predict the #deforestation of #rainforest and loss of biodiversity though the analysis of aerial photographs and #satellite data

✅ AI can be used to enhance the #sustainability of #agriculture, lower #airpollution or reduce negative environmental impact of infrastructure projects
  
AI can become a huge problem for climate change:
 
✅The use of AI technologies is expected to grow exponentially with the expected growth of the current global AI #market size of around $200 billion U.S. dollars to reach over 1.8 trillion U.S. dollars by 2030.

✅ #Machinelearning and the training of AI #algorithms require huge amount of computing power and #electricity

✅ The #computing #power required for AI applications, such as recognizing & processing images and vast among of data increased 300,000-fold from 2012 to 2018.

✅AI and #Deeplearning require huge amount of high-quality data and increasingly huge computing power and data #infrastructure

✅The training one AI model using a single high-end graphics card (#gpu ) generates the carbon equivalent of a flight across the United States or 626,000 pounds of carbon dioxide (MIT Technology Review

Huge Public Investments in AI for Good is needed to leverage the power of AI for climate action

✅ Increasingly AI models require and deep learning require huge computing power driven by specialized computer chips- called GPUs

✅ The costs of the needed AI infrastructure in the form of hyperscale #datacenters and data infrastructure are becoming huge

✅ Whereby #bigtech companies, such as Amazon, Google or Microsoft are investing billions into AI the public sector, research institutions and universities don’t have the necessary resources to make the necessary huge investments

✅ AI can only be unleased for climate action through public sector investments, since the big tech companies are purely focused on commercial applications of AI

✅ A large boost in public concessional #climatefinance is needed since only a very small part of private sector investments go into the development of AI models for the public good & AI to for climate action.

#tech #tech4good #deeptech @Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH @Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ)
